swissFromAbroad.metaTitle: You live abroad and own a flat in Switzerland: what tax is there?
swissFromAbroad.metaDescription: Owning property in Switzerland makes you taxable there even if you have never lived there. What is taxed, why an empty holiday flat still costs you, how much of your mortgage counts, and what changes in 2029.
swissFromAbroad.title: You live abroad and own a flat in Switzerland. What tax is there?
swissFromAbroad.lead: Everything written about Swiss tax and holiday flats is written for people who live in Switzerland and own something abroad. This is the other direction: your flat is in Switzerland and you are not.
points: Owning property in a Swiss canton makes you taxable in Switzerland, whatever your address and whatever your passport
Only the property is taxed. Your salary and savings at home are declared but not taxed
An empty holiday flat is taxed on the notional rent the canton assessed, not on what it earned
Only the Swiss share of your mortgage interest is deductible, in proportion to where your assets lie
From 1 January 2029 the notional rent disappears and cantons may tax second homes instead

sections.title: Yes, and your nationality has nothing to do with it
sections.body: Swiss law taxes a person where their real estate lies, whoever they are and wherever they live. Owning a flat or a house in a canton is enough on its own to create a tax liability there, which is why the municipality where the property stands sends you a tax return even though you have never lived in the country. Tax people call it limited liability: the property is taxed, not you as a whole.

sections.title: What Switzerland actually taxes
sections.body: Two things, and only two. The income from the property, which is either the rent you receive or a notional rent when you keep it for yourself. And the property as wealth, at the value the canton has put on it. Your salary abroad, your pension and your savings are not taxable in Switzerland and never become so because of the flat.

sections.title: The empty flat is the part people get wrong
sections.body: A holiday flat that stands empty eleven months of the year is taxed as though you had rented it to yourself. The canton assesses that notional rent, the Eigenmietwert, and it appears on the assessment notice along with the tax value. Nobody paid you anything and the tax is due anyway. A reduction is only considered when the property genuinely cannot be used, after a fire for example, and that is a conversation with the tax office rather than a box on the form.

sections.title: Nothing is estimated, because the canton already did it
sections.body: This is the good news. You do not have to value your own property or guess at a market rent: the cantonal assessment sets both the tax value and the notional rent, and the return simply wants those two figures. If you cannot find the notice, the municipal tax office where the property lies will send you a copy.

sections.title: Your mortgage is only partly deductible here
sections.body: Debts and debt interest are spread across everything you own, in proportion to where your assets lie. If the Swiss flat is a third of your worldwide assets, a third of your interest is deductible in Switzerland and the rest belongs to your own country. This is the single most common mistake, because an owner who deducts the whole Swiss mortgage has understated their Swiss income and will hear about it.

sections.title: Your income at home goes on the form, and is not taxed
sections.body: Switzerland taxes the flat at the rate that matches your total income and wealth, so the return asks for figures it has no intention of taxing. Leaving them out does not lower the bill, it invites the office to estimate them. For the federal tax there is also a floor: the rate is at least the one that matches the income earned in Switzerland, so a modest worldwide income does not buy you a near-zero rate.

sections.title: The post has to be able to reach you
sections.body: If you are abroad without anybody in Switzerland to receive your tax post, a decision can be served on you by publication in the cantonal official gazette, and the period for appealing it runs whether you saw it or not. The office will normally ask you to name an address for service here. A relative, a neighbour, the property manager or an adviser can all do it, and it is worth having one before you need it.

sections.title: What changes in 2029
sections.body: Switzerland voted in September 2025 to end the taxation of notional rent, and the Federal Council set the change in force for 1 January 2029. Second homes, which is what most property owned from abroad is, are the category cantons may tax instead with a new property tax. The deduction for maintenance costs goes at the same time. Until then the rules on this page apply unchanged.

sections.title: If you have never filed
sections.body: Waiting to be forgotten is not a strategy: ownership is recorded in the land register and the municipality knows exactly who you are. An office that hears nothing eventually assesses you at its own estimate, which is deliberately not generous and hard to overturn, and adds a fine for not filing. Catching up voluntarily costs less, and it is a case for an adviser rather than for a form filled in a hurry.

items.q: Does it matter that I am not Swiss?
items.a: No. Liability follows the property, not the passport. A Swiss citizen living in Berlin and a German citizen living in Berlin are in exactly the same position with regard to a flat in Zurich.

items.q: The flat is rented to tourists a few weeks a year. What then?
items.a: The rent you actually received replaces the notional rent for the period it was let, and the notional rent covers the rest of the year. Short-term letting can also bring cantonal or communal tourist taxes and, above certain thresholds, other obligations, which are separate from the tax return.

A gain on Swiss real estate is taxable in Switzerland, through a separate cantonal property gains tax rather than through this return. Your treaty will almost certainly leave that right with Switzerland, so plan for it before you sign anything.

items.q: Will my own country tax the flat as well?
items.a: Switzerland has the first right to tax property that stands in Switzerland. Your country of residence then either exempts it while still counting it when it sets your rate, or credits the Swiss tax against its own. Which of the two applies depends on your treaty with Switzerland, so check that at home. Nothing you file in Switzerland replaces your own return.

items.q: I live abroad. Why do I have to file in Switzerland at all?
items.a: Because the property is here. Swiss law makes an owner taxable in the place where the real estate lies, whatever their address (Art. 4 DBG for the federal tax, the same rule in the Zurich tax act). It is called limited liability: only the property is taxed, not you as a whole. The municipality where the property lies sends the return, and it is due even in a year when nothing happened with the flat.

items.q: Is my salary abroad taxed in Switzerland?
items.a: No. Only the property and its income are taxable here. Your salary, pension and other assets are asked for so that Switzerland can apply the rate that matches your full income and wealth to the Swiss part (Art. 7 Abs. 1 DBG). A larger income abroad therefore raises the rate on the flat, but never makes the income itself taxable here. For the federal tax there is also a floor: the rate is at least the one that matches the income earned in Switzerland (Art. 7 Abs. 2 DBG), so a small worldwide income does not buy a near-zero rate.

items.q: Where do I find the Eigenmietwert and the Steuerwert?
items.a: On the Schätzungsanzeige, the assessment notice the canton sends after a valuation, and on your last tax bill. Both figures are set by the canton, not by you and not by an estate agent. If you do not have the notice, ask the Gemeindesteueramt of the municipality where the property lies; they send a copy.

items.q: The flat is empty. Nobody lives there and it earns nothing.
items.a: It is still taxed on the Eigenmietwert, the rent the canton assumes you would otherwise pay. An empty holiday flat that is available to you counts as used by you. A reduction is only considered when the property truly cannot be used, for example after a fire, and that is a case for the tax office rather than for this tool.

items.q: I rent it out. What do I declare?
items.a: The rent you actually received over the year, without the utilities the tenant pays on top. That replaces the Eigenmietwert. You may then deduct either the flat 20% for maintenance and administration, or what you really spent if it was more, with receipts.

items.q: Can I deduct the interest on my mortgage?
items.a: Only part of it. Debts and debt interest are spread over everything you own, in proportion to where your assets lie. If the Zurich flat is a third of your assets worldwide, a third of your interest is deductible here. That is why the tool asks what you own elsewhere, and it is the single point most people get wrong.

{price} per property for your first declaration. In the following years it costs less, because your property is already set up. A Swiss adviser usually charges several hundred francs for the same work, every year.

The Zurich deadline is 31 March for the previous year. You can extend it online, free of charge, until 30 November. The extension is for filing, not for paying: interest runs on the tax from the general due date.

items.q: What happens if I do not file?
items.a: The office reminds you, then assesses you at its own estimate (Ermessensveranlagung). That estimate is deliberately not generous, it is hard to overturn, and it comes with a fine for not filing. Since ownership is recorded in the land register, waiting to be forgotten is not a strategy.

items.q: Do I need somebody in Switzerland to receive my post?
items.a: Somebody has to be able to reach you. Federal law says that if you are abroad without a representative in Switzerland, a decision can be served on you validly by publication in the cantonal official gazette (Art. 116 Abs. 2 DBG), and the appeal period then runs whether you saw it or not. The cantonal office will normally ask you to name a delivery address here, and it is in your own interest to have one: a relative, a neighbour, a property manager or an adviser.

items.q: Eigenmietwert is being abolished. What changes for me?
items.a: Parliament decided to end the taxation of notional rent, with the change taking effect on 1 January 2029. Second homes are meant to be covered instead by a new cantonal property tax, which is precisely the category most owners living abroad fall into. Until then the rules on this page apply unchanged, and we will update the tool when the cantonal rules are published.

spanishHoliday.metaTitle: Tax on a Spanish holiday home when you live somewhere else
spanishHoliday.metaDescription: Spain taxes a holiday home that earns nothing. How the imputed income of 1.1 or 2 percent of the cadastral value works, why living outside the EU costs you far more, and when the Modelo 210 is due.
spanishHoliday.title: The tax on a Spanish holiday home when you live somewhere else
spanishHoliday.lead: A flat in Spain that nobody rents out still produces a tax bill every year. Here is where the number comes from, and why two owners of identical flats can pay very different amounts.
points: Spain taxes an income nobody paid you: 1.1 percent of the cadastral value, or 2 percent where that value is older than ten years
The rate is 19 percent if you live in the EU or the EEA and 24 percent if you live anywhere else, Switzerland and the United Kingdom included
Only residents of another EU state may deduct costs. From outside, the mortgage, the community fee and the repairs count for nothing
Every co-owner files their own form, for their own share
IBI, the wealth tax and the Modelo 210 are three separate things

sections.title: Spain taxes the flat even when it is empty
sections.body: Spanish law taxes the possibility of using a property, not only the money it makes. If you are not tax resident in Spain and the flat is not let, a percentage of its cadastral value counts as your income for the year and is taxed. Only a habitual residence escapes this, and somebody who lives abroad does not have one in Spain. A flat you use for three weeks in August is taxed for the whole twelve months.

sections.title: Where the number comes from
sections.body: It starts with the cadastral value, which is on the IBI receipt the town hall sends every year. That value is not what the flat would sell for; it is usually far below the market price. The receipt also says when the value was last revised, and that decides your percentage: 1.1 percent where the revision took effect within the last ten tax periods, and 2 percent where it did not.

sections.title: Where you live decides your rate
sections.body: A resident of another EU state, or of Iceland, Norway or Liechtenstein, pays 19 percent. Everybody else pays 24 percent, and that includes Switzerland and the United Kingdom, which belong to neither. Your nationality is irrelevant: a Spaniard living in Zurich pays the same 24 percent as a Briton living in Zurich.

sections.title: From outside the EU you deduct nothing
sections.body: This is the difference that matters when the flat is let. A resident of another EU state may deduct the costs of earning the rent. Everybody else is taxed on the gross rent, with the mortgage interest, the community fee, the insurance and the repairs counting for nothing at all. Two neighbours with identical flats and identical tenants can end up paying very different tax purely because one of them lives inside the EU and the other does not.

sections.title: One form per owner
sections.body: Spain wants a Modelo 210 from each owner, for their own share, with their own NIE. A couple who own half each file two forms on half the value or half the rent, not one form between them. It is administrative rather than expensive, but it catches people out.

sections.title: When it is due
sections.body: For a flat you keep for yourself, the return for one year is due by 31 December of the next. For a let flat there is an annual window early in the following year. Both windows have moved in recent years, so check the current date rather than trusting an old article, including this one.

sections.title: IBI, wealth tax and Modelo 210 are not the same thing
sections.body: IBI is the municipal property tax, paid to the town hall, and it is the receipt that carries the cadastral value. Modelo 210 is the national income tax on the flat. And Spain also levies a wealth tax that can reach a non-resident owner of an expensive property, which is a third filing again. Paying one of them says nothing about the other two.

sections.title: If you have never filed
sections.body: Filing late of your own accord costs less than being found. Spain can go back several years and add a surcharge, and the tax office does eventually notice: your ownership is in the land register and the town hall bills you for IBI every year. If several years are open, that is a conversation with an adviser rather than a form filled in a hurry.

items.q: The flat earns nothing. Is there really tax?
items.a: Yes. That is the whole point of imputed income: the law taxes the use you could make of the property. The amounts are often modest, a few hundred euros a year on a typical holiday flat, which is exactly why people are surprised to learn they should have been paying it for a decade.

items.q: Where do I find the cadastral value?
items.a: On the annual IBI receipt from the town hall, which also gives the year of the last revision. The Catastro's own site shows it as well, with your NIE and a certificate. Do not use the purchase price: it is a different figure entirely.

items.q: I live in Switzerland. Is there really no way to deduct the mortgage?
items.a: Not against the Spanish tax. The deduction in the non-resident income tax act is written for residents of another EU state, and Switzerland is not one. It is worth knowing before you buy with a loan, because it changes the arithmetic of letting a Spanish flat considerably.

items.q: Do I declare the flat at home as well?
items.a: Usually yes. Spain has the first right to tax property that stands in Spain, and your own country then either exempts it while counting it for your rate or credits the Spanish tax. Which one applies is in your treaty with Spain.
